# sca security_key

[← Command reference](../commands.md)

`<sca_options>` are the [global options](../commands.md#global-options).

```text
The sca security key command help

The security key command is used for managing cryptographic token storage devices
- devices that securely store and utilize cryptographic information including
private keys and certificates.
```

**Syntax**

```text
sca [<sca_options>] security_key [<security_key_options>] <security_key_command>

security_key_options:

  -h, --help                    - display security key command help and exit

The security key command is one of the following:

  get_crt   - retrieving certificate for the given entity from a security key
  id        - retrieving ids of the currently inserted security key
  info      - show the status of every PIV slot on the security key
  init      - first time initialization of security_key
  openpgp_git - set up Git commit and tag signing with the OpenPGP signature key
  openpgp_key - create and back up OpenPGP keys, and move them to the YubiKey
  openpgp_ssh - set up SSH with the OpenPGP authentication key and gpg-agent
  unblock_pin - unblock a blocked pin with the stored puk, and update the pin file
  upload    - upload security document to security key
  verify    - test that an entity's private key on the security key can sign
  wait_for  - awaits for specific security key connection
```

**See also**

```text
type sca security_key <subcommand> --help for further information on each of the
security key related commands.
```

### Choosing a key: `--device SERIAL`

Every `security_key` subcommand except `openpgp_ssh`, `openpgp_git` and `openpgp_key create` accepts `--device SERIAL`, the YubiKey's hardware serial as printed by `sca security_key id` (or `ykman list --serials`). The serial is passed on to the tools: `yubico-piv-tool` is pointed at that key's reader, and `pkcs11-tool` at its `YubiKey PIV #<serial>` token.

- `info` and `verify`: with one key attached, `--device` is optional and nothing changes. With more than one attached and no `--device`, the command prints the attached serials and exits non-zero rather than pick one.
- `get_crt`, `init`, `unblock_pin`, `upload` and `wait_for`: these wait for the entity's configured key (`<entity>_security_key_id`). `--device` waits for the named key instead, which is how a second (backup) key of the same entity is reached. If no key is configured and more than one is attached, they refuse in the same way.
- `id`: lists only the named key, and fails if it is not attached.
- `openpgp_key to_card`: gpg writes to whichever OpenPGP card it finds, so `--device` is not passed on; `to_card` refuses unless that card has the given serial. Without `--device`, it refuses when more than one key is attached.

```bash
sca security_key id                         # 12345678 0
                                            # 87654321 1
sca security_key info --device 87654321
sca security_key upload --device 87654321 subca crt
```

If one attached reader's name is contained in another's, `yubico-piv-tool` cannot tell those two keys apart. In that case `sca` refuses and asks you to attach only the key you want to use.

**Subcommands**

- [get_crt](#sca-security_key-get_crt) - retrieving certificate for the given entity from a security key
- [id](#sca-security_key-id) - retrieving ids of the currently inserted security key
- [info](#sca-security_key-info) - show the status of every PIV slot on the security key
- [init](#sca-security_key-init) - first time initialization of security_key
- [openpgp_git](#sca-security_key-openpgp_git) - set up Git commit and tag signing with the OpenPGP signature key
- [openpgp_key](#sca-security_key-openpgp_key) - create and back up OpenPGP keys, and move them to the YubiKey
- [openpgp_ssh](#sca-security_key-openpgp_ssh) - set up SSH with the OpenPGP authentication key and gpg-agent
- [unblock_pin](#sca-security_key-unblock_pin) - unblock a blocked pin with the stored puk, and update the pin file
- [upload](#sca-security_key-upload) - upload security document to security key
- [verify](#sca-security_key-verify) - test that an entity's private key on the security key can sign
- [wait_for](#sca-security_key-wait_for) - awaits for specific security key connection

## sca security_key get_crt

```text
The security key get certificate command help

The security key get certificate command is used for retrieving certificate for
the given entity from a security key and according to the configuration.
```

**Syntax**

```text
sca [<sca_options>] security_key [<security_key_options>] get_crt [<get_crt_options>]

security_key_options:

  -h, --help                    - display security key command help and exit

get_crt_options:

  -h, --help                - print this help
  --device SERIAL           - use the security key with this serial instead of
                              the one configured for the entity. needed to
                              reach a second (backup) key of the same entity.
```

**Example:**
```bash
# Get sub-CA certificate from YubiKey
sca security_key get_crt subca
```

## sca security_key id

```text
The security key id command help

The security key id command is used for retrieving ids of the currently inserted
cryptographic token secure storage devices.

A security key id is the first 6 hexadecimal numbers of the token secure storage
device serial number, separated by dash '-' character.

The opensc card reader number associated with the security key is printed along
with the security key id with white space as a separator.

In case there are more than one security keys connected to the computer, they
will all be displayed one on each line.

In case there are no security keys connected to the system, dash sign is
displayed for both security key id and the card reader number.
```

**Syntax**

```text
sca [<sca_options>] security_key [<security_key_options>] id [<id_options>]

security_key_options:

  -h, --help                    - display security key command help and exit

id_options:

  -h, --help                - print this help
  -t, --security-key-type   - retrieve security keys only for security keys of
                              specified type. currently supported type is
                              yubikey only.
  --device SERIAL           - list only the security key with this serial, and
                              exit with an error if it is not attached.
```

Useful for identifying which key is inserted when you have multiple YubiKeys: each attached key is printed on its own line as `<serial> <reader number>`.

## sca security_key info

```text
The security key info command help

The security key info command displays the status of all PIV slots on a connected
YubiKey, including certificate details and private key presence.

For each populated slot, it shows the certificate subject, expiration date, and
whether a private key is present. This is useful for verifying YubiKey contents
and diagnosing issues with key storage.
```

**Syntax**

```text
sca [<sca_options>] security_key [<security_key_options>] info [<info_options>]

security_key_options:

  -h, --help                    - display security key command help and exit

info_options:

  -h, --help                - print this help
  --device SERIAL           - act on the security key with this serial. when
                              more than one key is attached, it is required:
                              the command lists the attached serials and
                              exits rather than pick one.
```

**Example output:**
```
YubiKey PIV Slot Information
============================

Slot 9c (Digital Signature):
  Subject:   MyCompany SubCA - admin
  Expires:   Jan 21 19:16:13 2036 GMT
  Algorithm: rsaEncryption

Slot 82 (Retired Key 1 (CA)):
  Subject:   MyCompany CA
  Expires:   Jan 21 19:44:49 2036 GMT
  Algorithm: rsaEncryption
```

## sca security_key init

```text
The security key init command help

The security key init command is used for first time initialization of the
currently inserted cryptographic token secure storage device as well as for
security key access keys.

A security key initialization consists of setting the three security key access
keys: pin, puk and the management key. The passwords are randomly generated and
saved to the keys file-system.

You should write down the pin and remember the pin. It's 6 digits that you will
need to use to access the keys stored on the token device.

It is good to have the management key somewhere on paper as well although it is
best used only in air-gapped environment where it's safe to attach the keys
file-system.

Rolling (assigning new values to) the access keys is also performed by this
command when ran with appropriate parameters.

init supports security_key_type 'yubikey' only; for 'pkcs11' tokens set the
pin, puk and management key with the token's own tools.

IMPORTANT NOTE: this command shall be run in an air-gapped (offline,
disconnected from the internet) environment.
```

**Syntax**

```text
sca [<sca_options>] security_key [<security_key_options>] init [<init_options>] <entity>

security_key_options:

  -h, --help                    - display security key command help and exit

init_options:

  -h, --help      - print this help
  -r, --roll-keys - change security key access keys (pin/puk/management key) by
                    setting the new ones randomly generated
  --device SERIAL - use the security key with this serial instead of the one
                    configured for the entity. needed to reach a second
                    (backup) key of the same entity.

The entity parameter is the type of the entity for which we want to initialize
the security key for. The sca configuration file assigns a cryptographic token
storage device (a security key) to each of the declared default entity types
(ca, subca, user, service, host). The related setting name is:
<entity>_security_key_id.
```

**What it does:**
- Generates a new random management key, PIN and PUK, and sets them on the key
  (replacing the factory defaults, or the current values with `--roll-keys`)
- Stores them in `~/.sca/keys/<ca>/<subca>/private/` (created if missing,
  mode 0700) as `<prefix>yubikey-{key,pin,puk}.txt`, mode 0600. With
  `--roll-keys` the previous files are kept as `*.bak`
- If setting a value fails, the files still match what is on the key: when
  nothing changed they are left as they were; when only part changed, they
  record the new values for what changed, and the error says which ones

**Important:** Save the generated credentials! You'll need the PUK if you forget your PIN.

## sca security_key openpgp_git

```text
The security key openpgp_git command help

The security key openpgp_git command sets up Git to sign commits and tags with
the signature key of the YubiKey's OpenPGP applet, and prints that key's public
key for the Git host. It needs no sca configuration.

setup reads the signature key's fingerprint from the card (gpg --card-status),
checks that its public key is in the local GnuPG keyring, and sets
user.signingkey to <fingerprint>!, commit.gpgsign and tag.gpgSign to true, in
the global git config (or, with --local, the current repository's). Settings
that already have the right value are left alone. If any setting has another
value, gpg.format included, setup lists each one with the command that accepts
the new value, and changes nothing. It prints the GPG_TTY line for the shell
startup file, but edits no shell files.

public_key prints the armored public key (gpg --armor --export) for the GPG
keys page of GitHub or GitLab, so signed commits show as verified.

gpg runs with --batch: sca never asks for, reads or logs the OpenPGP PIN. If gpg
is missing, install the OpenPGP packages with sca install --openpgp.
```

**Syntax**

```text
sca [<sca_options>] security_key [<security_key_options>] openpgp_git setup [<setup_options>]
sca [<sca_options>] security_key [<security_key_options>] openpgp_git public_key [<public_key_options>]

security_key_options:

  -h, --help                    - display security key command help and exit

setup_options:

  -h, --help          - print this help
  --local             - set up the current repository only (git config
                        --local), rather than every repository (git config
                        --global, the default)
  --no-tags           - sign commits only: leave tag.gpgSign alone
  -n, --dry-run       - print what would change, and change nothing

public_key_options:

  -h, --help          - print this help
  -o, --output FILE   - write the public key to FILE rather than stdout. an
                        existing FILE is never overwritten
```

**What it does:**
- `setup`: reads the signature key's fingerprint from `gpg --card-status --with-colons` and checks with `gpg --list-keys` that its public key is in the keyring
- `setup` then sets `user.signingkey <fingerprint>!`, `commit.gpgsign true` and `tag.gpgSign true` (not with `--no-tags`) with `git config --global`, which honours `GIT_CONFIG_GLOBAL`, or with `git config --local` given `--local`. Only that scope is read and written, and `gpg.program` is never set
- Settings already right are left alone (`yes`, `on` and `1` count as true; the key is compared ignoring case). If any setting has another value, or `gpg.format` is set to something other than `openpgp` (e.g. SSH signing), `setup` lists them all with the `git config` command that accepts each, writes nothing and exits 1. `-n`, `--dry-run` prints what would change and changes nothing
- `setup` warns when `user.email` is not a user ID of the key (the Git host would show commits as Unverified), prints the `export GPG_TTY="$(tty)"` line for the shell startup file, and edits no shell files
- `public_key`: runs `gpg --armor --export <fingerprint>`, the primary key with all its subkeys. `-o FILE` writes it to FILE instead of stdout, and never overwrites an existing file
- Neither mode needs `sca config`, and gpg runs with `--batch`, so sca never asks for or sees the OpenPGP PIN

**Example:**
```bash
sca install --openpgp                         # gnupg, scdaemon, ykman
sca security_key openpgp_git setup --dry-run
sca security_key openpgp_git setup
echo 'export GPG_TTY="$(tty)"' >> ~/.bashrc
sca security_key openpgp_git public_key -o ~/gpg-signing.asc   # for GitHub or GitLab
git commit --allow-empty -m test && git log --show-signature -1
```

See [GPG with a YubiKey](../gpg-yubikey.md#54-git-commit-and-tag-signing) for the manual steps, and [section 3](../gpg-yubikey.md#3-keys) to put a signature key on the card.

## sca security_key openpgp_key

```text
The security key openpgp_key command help

The security key openpgp_key command creates an OpenPGP key with an offline
master key, backs it up, and moves its subkeys to the YubiKey's OpenPGP applet,
as in docs/gpg-yubikey.md section 3 option B. It needs no sca configuration.

create makes a certify-only master key that never expires, and a signing,
an encryption and an authentication subkey, in the GnuPG home (GNUPGHOME). It
writes master-and-subkeys.asc, subkeys.asc, public.asc and revoke.asc (the
revocation certificate) with mode 600 to the backup folder, by default
~/.sca/keys/openpgp/<fingerprint>, and never overwrites a file there. Run it
on an offline machine, such as the sca air-gapped USB stick; it needs no card.

to_card moves the three subkeys to the signature, encryption and
authentication slots of the card, then saves, which deletes their secrets
from the disk. It refuses when more than one YubiKey is attached (unless
--device names the one gpg will write to), when a slot already holds a key
(unless --force), when there is no backup of the key (unless
--no-backup-check), and when ed25519 keys meet firmware before 5.2.3. If any
step fails it quits without saving, so the subkeys stay on the disk. It does
not change the touch policy: see ykman openpgp keys set-touch.

gpg's pinentry asks for the passphrase and the admin PIN. For unattended runs,
--passphrase-file and --admin-pin-file give them in files instead; sca sends
them to gpg through a pipe, never on a command line or to the log. If gpg is
missing, install the OpenPGP packages with sca install --openpgp.
```

**Syntax**

```text
sca [<sca_options>] security_key [<security_key_options>] openpgp_key create --name NAME --email EMAIL [<create_options>]
sca [<sca_options>] security_key [<security_key_options>] openpgp_key to_card [<to_card_options>]

security_key_options:

  -h, --help                    - display security key command help and exit

create_options:

  -h, --help              - print this help
  --name NAME             - the name in the user ID (required)
  --email EMAIL           - the email in the user ID (required)
  --algo ALGO             - ed25519 (default; ed25519, cv25519 and ed25519
                            subkeys) or rsa4096, for firmware before 5.2.3
  --expire WHEN           - when the subkeys expire: never, a number of days,
                            or Nd, Nw, Nm, Ny, or YYYY-MM-DD (default 2y). the
                            master key never expires
  --backup-dir DIR        - write the backup files to DIR, rather than
                            ~/.sca/keys/openpgp/<fingerprint>
  --passphrase-file FILE  - read the key's passphrase from FILE (one line),
                            rather than asking with pinentry

to_card_options:

  -h, --help              - print this help
  --device SERIAL         - the YubiKey to write to. gpg's card must have
                            this serial, so other keys may stay attached only
                            if gpg does not pick them
  --fingerprint FPR       - the key whose subkeys to move. by default, the
                            only key with one [S], [E] and [A] subkey on disk
  --backup-dir DIR        - where to look for master-and-subkeys.asc, rather
                            than ~/.sca/keys/openpgp/<fingerprint>
  --force                 - replace keys already in the card's slots
  --no-backup-check       - move the subkeys without a backup file
  --passphrase-file FILE  - read the key's passphrase from FILE (one line)
  --admin-pin-file FILE   - read the card's admin PIN from FILE (one line)
```

**What it does:**
- `create`: checks `--name`, `--email`, `--algo` and `--expire`, and refuses before making anything if a backup file already exists in `--backup-dir`
- `create` then runs `gpg --quick-generate-key "NAME <EMAIL>" <algo> cert never`, reads the fingerprint from the `KEY_CREATED` status line, and adds the subkeys with `gpg --quick-add-key <FPR> <algo> sign|encr|auth <expire>` (ed25519: `ed25519`, `cv25519`, `ed25519`; rsa4096: `rsa4096` for all three)
- `create` writes `master-and-subkeys.asc` (`--export-secret-keys`), `subkeys.asc` (`--export-secret-subkeys`), `public.asc` (`--export`) and `revoke.asc` (a copy of `openpgp-revocs.d/<FPR>.rev` in the GnuPG home), each through a temporary file with mode 600 and `mv -n`, to `~/.sca/keys/openpgp/<FPR>/` or `--backup-dir`. Folders it creates have mode 700. If a file can't be written, it names the ones that were and weren't, and leaves the key in place
- `to_card`: picks the key (`--fingerprint`, or the only one with a `[C]` master and exactly one `[S]`, `[E]` and `[A]` subkey on disk, not expired or revoked), and reads `gpg --card-status --with-colons`
- `to_card` refuses, before writing anything, when: `--device` is not the serial of the card gpg sees; there is no `--device` and `ykman list --serials` shows more than one key (or ykman is missing); an ed25519 or cv25519 subkey meets firmware before 5.2.3 (`ykman info`); a target slot is filled and there is no `--force`; `master-and-subkeys.asc` in the backup folder is missing or holds another key and there is no `--no-backup-check`
- `to_card` then runs one `gpg --edit-key <FPR> --command-fd 0 --status-fd 1` session: `key N`, `keytocard` and the slot (1 signature, 2 encryption, 3 authentication) for each subkey, then `save`. Any unexpected prompt, failure or repeated secret request makes it `quit` without saving, and it reports which slots were already written. Afterwards each subkey must be a card stub (`ssb>`)
- Without `--passphrase-file` and `--admin-pin-file` sca never sees a secret: gpg's pinentry asks. With them, gpg runs with `--pinentry-mode loopback`; `create` passes the passphrase file to gpg, and `to_card` sends each secret through the `--command-fd` pipe only when gpg asks for it, never in argv, the environment of a command or `~/.sca/log`
- Neither mode needs `sca config`, and the touch policy is left alone

**Example:**
```bash
sca install --openpgp                            # gnupg, scdaemon, ykman
# on the offline machine
export GNUPGHOME="$(mktemp -d)"
sca security_key openpgp_key create --name "Alice Example" --email alice@example.com
# copy ~/.sca/keys/openpgp/<FPR>/ and $GNUPGHOME to an encrypted offline drive
sca security_key openpgp_key to_card --device 12345678
ykman openpgp keys set-touch sig on              # optional, see section 4
sca security_key openpgp_key create --name "CI Test" --email ci@example.com \
  --passphrase-file pass.txt --backup-dir ./backup
sca security_key openpgp_key to_card --device 12345678 --backup-dir ./backup \
  --passphrase-file pass.txt --admin-pin-file admin-pin.txt   # unattended
```

See [GPG with a YubiKey](../gpg-yubikey.md#option-b-offline-master-key-recommended) for what the commands do by hand, and [touch policies](../gpg-yubikey.md#4-touch-policies).

## sca security_key openpgp_ssh

```text
The security key openpgp_ssh command help

The security key openpgp_ssh command sets up SSH with the authentication key of
the YubiKey's OpenPGP applet, served by gpg-agent in place of ssh-agent, and
prints that key's SSH public key. It needs no sca configuration.

setup adds enable-ssh-support to gpg-agent.conf in the GnuPG home folder
(gpgconf --list-dirs homedir, which honours GNUPGHOME), once, and restarts
gpg-agent only when it added it, since a restart drops the cached PIN. It then
prints the shell lines that point SSH_AUTH_SOCK at gpg-agent (sh, bash and zsh
syntax; fish is not covered), and with --shell-rc FILE appends the ones FILE
does not have yet. It never edits ~/.ssh/config, but prints the Match line
that keeps the PIN prompt in the current terminal.

public_key reads the authentication key's fingerprint from the card
(gpg --card-status) and prints its SSH public key (gpg --export-ssh-key), for
the server's ~/.ssh/authorized_keys. The public key must be in the local GnuPG
keyring.

gpg runs with --batch: sca never asks for, reads or logs the OpenPGP PIN. If gpg
or gpgconf is missing, install the OpenPGP packages with sca install --openpgp.
```

**Syntax**

```text
sca [<sca_options>] security_key [<security_key_options>] openpgp_ssh setup [<setup_options>]
sca [<sca_options>] security_key [<security_key_options>] openpgp_ssh public_key [<public_key_options>]

security_key_options:

  -h, --help                    - display security key command help and exit

setup_options:

  -h, --help          - print this help
  --shell-rc FILE     - append the shell lines to FILE (e.g. ~/.bashrc),
                        skipping any it already has. FILE is created if
                        missing
  -n, --dry-run       - print what would change, and change nothing

public_key_options:

  -h, --help          - print this help
  -o, --output FILE   - write the public key to FILE rather than stdout. an
                        existing FILE is never overwritten
```

**What it does:**
- `setup`: appends `enable-ssh-support` to `gpg-agent.conf` in the GnuPG home folder (`gpgconf --list-dirs homedir`, so `GNUPGHOME` is honoured) unless it is already there, and then runs `gpgconf --kill gpg-agent`. When the option is already there the agent is left running, so its cached PIN is kept
- `setup` prints the shell lines to add (sh, bash and zsh syntax). `--shell-rc FILE` appends the ones FILE doesn't already have, after a `# added by sca security_key openpgp_ssh setup` comment
- `setup` prints the `~/.ssh/config` line `Match host * exec "gpg-connect-agent updatestartuptty /bye"` but never edits `~/.ssh/config`. `-n`, `--dry-run` prints what would change and changes nothing
- `public_key`: reads the authentication key's fingerprint from `gpg --card-status --with-colons` and runs `gpg --export-ssh-key <fingerprint>!`. `-o FILE` writes the key to FILE instead of stdout, and never overwrites an existing file
- Neither mode needs `sca config`, and gpg runs with `--batch`, so sca never asks for or sees the OpenPGP PIN

**Example:**
```bash
sca install --openpgp                         # gnupg, scdaemon, ykman
sca security_key openpgp_ssh setup --shell-rc ~/.bashrc
. ~/.bashrc
ssh-add -L                                    # cardno:... key
sca security_key openpgp_ssh public_key -o ~/.ssh/id_gpg.pub
```

See [SSH with a YubiKey](../ssh-yubikey-options.md#openpgp-gpg-agent-ssh) for when to choose OpenPGP, and [GPG with a YubiKey](../gpg-yubikey.md#3-keys) to put an authentication key on the card.

## sca security_key unblock_pin

```text
The security key unblock_pin command help

The security key unblock_pin command recovers a PIV pin that is blocked after
too many wrong attempts, using the puk sca stored when the security key was
initialized, and keeps sca's pin file in step with the key.

By default a new random pin is set on the key and, once the key has taken it,
written to the entity's pin file (mode 0600). With --keep-pin the pin already
in the pin file is set again instead, and the file is not changed.

The puk is tried once only. If the puk file is missing, or the key refuses the
puk, the command stops, leaves the pin file as it was, and says how many puk
retries remain. A blocked puk leaves only a reset of the PIV application, which
destroys its keys; see docs/yubikey.md.
```

**Syntax**

```text
sca [<sca_options>] security_key [<security_key_options>] unblock_pin [<unblock_pin_options>] <entity>

security_key_options:

  -h, --help                    - display security key command help and exit

unblock_pin_options:

  -h, --help      - print this help
  -k, --keep-pin  - set the pin already in the pin file again, rather than a
                    new random one
  --device SERIAL - use the security key with this serial instead of the one
                    configured for the entity. needed to reach a second
                    (backup) key of the same entity.

entity is one of: ca, subca, user, service, host
```

**What it does:**
- Reads the PUK from `<prefix>yubikey-puk.txt` and runs `yubico-piv-tool -a unblock-pin` on the entity's key
- By default sets a new random PIN and, once the key has taken it, writes it to `<prefix>yubikey-pin.txt` (mode 0600)
- `-k`, `--keep-pin`: set the PIN already in the PIN file again; the file is not changed
- The PUK is tried once only. If the PUK file is missing, or the key refuses the PUK, it stops with the PIN file unchanged and says how many PUK retries remain. A blocked PUK leaves only a [PIV reset](../yubikey.md#reset-piv-emergency), which destroys the keys on it

**Example:**
```bash
sca security_key verify subca         # FAILED ... PIN error (wrong PIN or PIN blocked)
sca security_key unblock_pin subca
sca security_key verify subca         # SUCCESS
```

## sca security_key upload

```text
The security key upload command help

The security key upload command is used for uploading a security document into a
cryptographic token secure storage device.

The security documents that are stored in security keys include private keys and
certificates. Each security key device can hold one or more private key - certificate
pairs. For example, yubikey 4 can keep 25 such pairs.

Unless the force flag had been specified, the upload will fail in case the
target security key storage slot has been already occupied by certificate/key.
Forcing replacing the current values in the security key storage slot.
```

**Syntax**

```text
sca [<sca_options>] security_key [<security_key_options>] upload [<upload_options>] <entity> <document>

security_key_options:

  -h, --help                    - display security key command help and exit

upload_options:

  -h, --help      - print this help
  -f, --force     - force will replace any existing key or certificate in the
                    target security key storage slot.
  --device SERIAL - use the security key with this serial instead of the one
                    configured for the entity. needed to reach a second
                    (backup) key of the same entity.

entity may be either ca, subca, user, host or service
document may be either crt (for certificate) or key (for private key)
```

Each call uploads one document, so uploading both the certificate and the private key takes two calls.

The target slot is derived from the entity's `pkcs11_id` setting (e.g. `02` → slot 9c for the sub-CA default, `05` → slot 82 for the CA default). See [PIV Slots](../yubikey.md#piv-slots).

**Example:**
```bash
# Upload sub-CA certificate and private key to YubiKey
sca security_key upload subca crt
sca security_key upload subca key
```

After upload, the private key on disk can be securely deleted - all signing operations will use the YubiKey.

---

## sca security_key verify

```text
The security key verify command help

The security key verify command tests whether a private key is present and
functional on the YubiKey for a given entity. It does this by attempting to
sign test data with the key.

This is the only reliable way to detect private key presence, as tools like
ykman and yubico-piv-tool may incorrectly report keys as missing due to
display bugs.
```

**Syntax**

```text
sca [<sca_options>] security_key [<security_key_options>] verify [<verify_options>] <entity>

security_key_options:

  -h, --help                    - display security key command help and exit

verify_options:

  -h, --help                - print this help
  --device SERIAL           - act on the security key with this serial. when
                              more than one key is attached, it is required:
                              the command lists the attached serials and
                              exits rather than pick one.

entity is one of: ca, subca, user, service, host
```

**Example:**
```bash
# Verify sub-CA private key on YubiKey
sca security_key verify subca

# Verify CA private key (if stored on YubiKey)
sca security_key verify ca
```

This is the most reliable way to confirm a key exists, as tools like `ykman piv info` may incorrectly report "Private key: Not present" even when keys are working.

The ykcs11 module path comes from the `ykcs11_module` config setting. If that file doesn't exist, this host's library folders are searched before failing (see [Library Paths](../configuration.md#library-paths)). See [YubiKey Setup](../yubikey.md#verify-private-key-presence).

---

## sca security_key wait_for

```text
The security key wait for command help

The security key wait for command is used for pausing execution of a program and
prompting a user to insert particular security key device.

A security key wait for is used internally by sca and may be useful in custom
tools for management of security keys.

At a terminal it waits as long as it takes. Run unattended (stdin is not a
terminal) it gives up after 10 seconds instead of waiting forever, and fails
with an error naming the key it waited for and the keys it saw. Use --timeout
or security_key_wait_timeout to change the limit.

The last output line is the number of the smart card reader through in which
the awaited security key resides.
```

**Syntax**

```text
sca [<sca_options>] security_key [<security_key_options>] wait_for [<wait_for_options>] <entity>

security_key_options:

  -h, --help                    - display security key command help and exit

wait_for_options:

  -h, --help        - print this help
  --device SERIAL   - use the security key with this serial instead of the one
                      configured for the entity. needed to reach a second
                      (backup) key of the same entity.
  --timeout SECONDS - give up and fail after SECONDS when the key is not
                      attached. 0 waits forever. when not given, the
                      security_key_wait_timeout variable (from the environment
                      or an export line in sca.config) is used; when that is
                      not set either, there is no limit if stdin is a
                      terminal, and the limit is 10 seconds if it is not (a
                      script, ci, a pipe).
```

The key is identified by the serial configured in `<entity>_security_key_id`, or the one given with `--device`. Useful in scripts.

**Example:**
```bash
# Wait for the sub-CA's configured YubiKey
sca security_key wait_for subca

# Wait for the sub-CA's backup YubiKey, serial 12345678
sca security_key wait_for --device 12345678 subca

# Unattended (script, CI): fail after 30 s instead of the default 10 s
sca security_key wait_for --timeout 30 subca < /dev/null

# Or set the limit for every command that waits for a key (0 waits forever)
export security_key_wait_timeout=30
```
